nodes.name: Discovery
nodes.statement: Such a finding is referred to as a \textit{discovery}.

nodes.name: Number of hypotheses m and of true nulls m_0
nodes.statement: Denote by $m$ the total number of hypotheses (e.g., the number of genes whose expression levels were measured), and assume that the null hypothesis is true for $m_0$ out of the $m$ (i.e., $m_0$ genes' expression levels do not differentiate the two types).

nodes.name: Number of false nulls m_1
nodes.statement: For $m_1=m-m_0$ the null hypothesis is false (the expression levels of types $A$ and $B$ are sampled from different distributions).

nodes.name: p-values p_i
nodes.statement: A~statistical test is performed independently for each variable, producing a~$p$-value $p_i$, $i=1,2,\ldots,m$.

nodes.name: Number of rejections R
nodes.statement: On the basis of some thresholding operation on the $p_i$'s, the null hypothesis is rejected for $R$ tests.

nodes.name: False discovery (type I error)
nodes.statement: The decision to reject (or not) can be correct or false; When the null hypothesis is rejected for one of the $m_0$ variables for which it is actually true, we have a~``false discovery'' (type I error).
differentia: the null hypothesis is rejected for one of the $m_0$ variables for which it is actually true

nodes.name: False Discovery Rate (FDR)
nodes.statement: Out of the $R$ rejected hypotheses, the fraction $V/R$ is falsely rejected. The expected value of this fraction was termed by \citet{BH95} (referred to as BH95) as the False Discovery Rate (FDR), \begin{equation} \mathit{FDR} \equiv E \biggl( \frac{V}{R} \Big| R >0 \biggr) \Pr(R>0) \equiv E \biggl(\frac{V}{R^+} \biggr), \end{equation} where here and later in the paper the term $R^{+} \equiv \max(R,1)$ is used for brevity.
nodes.statement_short: FDR $=E(V/R^+)$, the expected fraction of false rejections among rejections, with $R^+=\max(R,1)$.

nodes.name: FDR definition
nodes.statement: \mathit{FDR} \equiv E \biggl( \frac{V}{R} \Big| R >0 \biggr) \Pr(R>0) \equiv E \biggl(\frac{V}{R^+} \biggr),
nodes.label: eq:defFDR

nodes.name: Benjamini-Hochberg (BH95) step-up procedure
nodes.statement: The original BH95 procedure to control the FDR is given as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Denote by $q$ the desired level, $0<q \leq1$, of the FDR and define the following set of constants: \begin{equation} \alpha_i=\frac{iq}{m}, \qquad i=1,2,\ldots,m. \end{equation} \item Sort the $p$-values $p_i$ and relabel the hypotheses accordingly, $p_{(1)}\leq p_{(2)}\leq\cdots\leq p_{(m)}$, such that $(i)$ is the index of the hypothesis with the $i$th smallest $p$-value. \item Identify $R$ as \begin{equation} R=\max \bigl\{i\dvtx p_{(i)}\leq\alpha_i \bigr\}. \end{equation} If no such $R \geq1$ exists, no hypothesis is rejected; otherwise reject all $R$ hypotheses $(i)=1,2,\ldots,R$. \end{enumerate}
input: the desired level, $0<q \leq1$, of the FDR
nodes.statement_short: Sort the p-values and reject the R smallest, where R is the largest i with $p_{(i)}\le iq/m$.

nodes.name: BH95 constants alpha_i = iq/m
nodes.statement: \alpha_i=\frac{iq}{m}, \qquad i=1,2,\ldots,m.
nodes.label: eq:alphadef

nodes.name: Fix level q and constants alpha_i
nodes.statement: Denote by $q$ the desired level, $0<q \leq1$, of the FDR and define the following set of constants: \begin{equation} \alpha_i=\frac{iq}{m}, \qquad i=1,2,\ldots,m. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fix the level $q$ and the constants $\alpha_i=iq/m$.

nodes.name: Sort the p-values
nodes.statement: Sort the $p$-values $p_i$ and relabel the hypotheses accordingly, $p_{(1)}\leq p_{(2)}\leq\cdots\leq p_{(m)}$, such that $(i)$ is the index of the hypothesis with the $i$th smallest $p$-value.
nodes.statement_short: Sort the p-values

nodes.name: Select R and reject
nodes.statement: Identify $R$ as \begin{equation} R=\max \bigl\{i\dvtx p_{(i)}\leq\alpha_i \bigr\}. \end{equation} If no such $R \geq1$ exists, no hypothesis is rejected; otherwise reject all $R$ hypotheses $(i)=1,2,\ldots,R$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $R=\max\{i: p_{(i)}\le\alpha_i\}$ and reject the $R$ smallest p-values.

nodes.name: BH95 step-up rule R
nodes.statement: R=\max \bigl\{i\dvtx p_{(i)}\leq\alpha_i \bigr\}.
nodes.label: eq:alpha

nodes.name: Step-up and step-down procedures
nodes.statement: It is referred to in BH95 as ``\textit{step-up}''; in general, there could be more than one intersection point [of the $p_{(i)}$ and $\alpha_i$ lines], in which case the step-up procedure identifies the intersection with the largest $p$-value as $R$, whereas the more conservative ``\textit{step-down}'' procedure identifies the lowest one, replacing equation (\ref{eq:alpha}) by \begin{equation} R=\min \bigl\{i\dvtx p_{(i)} > \alpha_i \bigr\} - 1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Step-up takes the largest intersection of $p_{(i)}$ with $\alpha_i$ as $R$; step-down takes $R=\min\{i:p_{(i)}>\alpha_i\}-1$.

nodes.name: Step-down rule
nodes.statement: R=\min \bigl\{i\dvtx p_{(i)} > \alpha_i \bigr\} - 1.
nodes.label: eq:alpha_step_down

nodes.name: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR bound
nodes.statement: The bound \begin{equation} \mathit{FDR} = E \biggl(\frac{V}{R^+} \biggr) \leq\frac{m_0}{m}q \end{equation} was proved by BH95 for independent tests, and by \citet{BY2001} for a certain type of ``positive dependency'' called PRDS (\textit{Positive Regression Dependency on each one from a Subset}).
assumptions: for independent tests
for a certain type of ``positive dependency'' called PRDS
conclusions: \mathit{FDR} = E \biggl(\frac{V}{R^+} \biggr) \leq\frac{m_0}{m}q
nodes.statement_short: The BH95 procedure has $FDR\le (m_0/m)q$ for independent tests (BH95) and under PRDS dependence (Benjamini-Yekutieli).

nodes.name: BH95 bound FDR <= m_0 q/m
nodes.statement: \mathit{FDR} = E \biggl(\frac{V}{R^+} \biggr) \leq\frac{m_0}{m}q
nodes.label: eq:BH95

nodes.name: BH95 controls the FDR at level q
nodes.statement: The value of $m_0$ is unknown to the researcher, but since $m_0 \leq m$, this procedure leads to the bound \begin{equation} \mathit{FDR} = E \biggl(\frac{V}{R^+} \biggr) \leq\frac{m_0}{m}q \leq q. \end{equation}
assumptions: since $m_0 \leq m$
conclusions: \mathit{FDR} = E \biggl(\frac{V}{R^+} \biggr) \leq\frac{m_0}{m}q \leq q.

nodes.name: BH95 bound FDR <= q
nodes.statement: \mathit{FDR} = E \biggl(\frac{V}{R^+} \biggr) \leq\frac{m_0}{m}q \leq q.
nodes.label: eq:FDR95

nodes.name: Oracle constants alpha'_i and oracle rejection number R'
nodes.statement: Clearly, had we known $m_0$, we could have defined a different set of constants [compare to equation (\ref{eq:alphadef})] \begin{equation} \alpha'_i=\frac{iq}{m_0} \end{equation} and defining \begin{equation} R^\prime=\max \bigl\{i\dvtx p_{(i)}\leq\alpha'_i \bigr\} \end{equation} would have obtained a larger number $R^\prime\geq R$ of rejected hypotheses (still with $\mathit{FDR} \leq q$) than the number $R$ given by the original BH95 procedure, which used $m$ as an upper-bound on $m_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Knowing $m_0$, use $\alpha'_i=iq/m_0$ and $R'=\max\{i:p_{(i)}\le\alpha'_i\}\ge R$, still with FDR $\le q$.

nodes.name: Oracle constants alpha'_i = iq/m_0
nodes.statement: \alpha'_i=\frac{iq}{m_0}
nodes.label: eq:alphaprime

nodes.name: Oracle rejection number R'
nodes.statement: R^\prime=\max \bigl\{i\dvtx p_{(i)}\leq\alpha'_i \bigr\}
nodes.label: eq:alphapp

nodes.name: Oracle procedure (ORC)
nodes.statement: This procedure, based on knowledge of $m_0$, is called ``oracle'' (ORC); see \citet{gavrilov2009}.

nodes.name: Adaptive (improved) FDR procedures
nodes.statement: Subsequently, various improved (also called ``adaptive'') procedures were proposed, based on the idea of estimating the unknown $m_0$ in order to get a more accurate handle on the FDR.
differentia: based on the idea of estimating the unknown $m_0$

nodes.name: Local FDR estimation procedures and the estimator condition (9)
nodes.statement: Procedures for local FDR \textit{estimation}: This approach, previously suggested and applied by \citet{yekutieli1999}, \citet{storey2002} and \citet{poundscheng2006}, can be used when one has an estimator $\hat{m}_0$ of~$m_0$ that satisfies \begin{equation} m_0\leq E(\hat{m}_0)\leq m. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Local FDR estimation uses an estimator $\hat m_0$ of $m_0$ with $m_0\le E(\hat m_0)\le m$.

nodes.name: Estimator condition m_0 <= E(hat m_0) <= m
nodes.statement: m_0\leq E(\hat{m}_0)\leq m.
nodes.label: eq:mhat_condition

nodes.name: Local FDR (lFDR) estimate t_(i)
nodes.statement: In procedures of this type one can write the local FDR (lFDR) estimate as [see \citet{poundscheng2006}] \begin{equation} t_{(i)}=\frac{\hat{v}(p_{(i)})}{\hat{F}(p_{(i)})}, \end{equation} where $p_{(i)}$ is the ordered $p$-value, $\hat{v}(\alpha)$ is the estimator for the type I errors (in the rejection region), and $\hat{F}(\alpha)$ is the estimator for the probability $\Pr(p\leq\alpha)$ [often estimated for $p_{(i)}$ by $i/m$].
nodes.statement_short: The lFDR estimate is $t_{(i)}=\hat v(p_{(i)})/\hat F(p_{(i)})$, estimated type I errors over estimated $\Pr(p\le\alpha)$.

nodes.name: An estimator satisfying (9) improves the local-FDR estimator
nodes.statement: Since for $\hat{v}(\alpha)$ most methods use \begin{equation} \hat{v}(\alpha)=\alpha\frac{\hat{m}_0}{m}, \end{equation} any estimator that satisfies equation (\ref{eq:mhat_condition}) can provide an improved estimator for the local-FDR by \begin{equation} \alpha\frac{m_0}{m}\leq E(\hat{v}(\alpha))=\alpha\frac{E(\hat{m}_0 )}{m}\leq\alpha. \end{equation}
assumptions: for $\hat{v}(\alpha)$ most methods use
any estimator that satisfies equation (\ref{eq:mhat_condition})
conclusions: \alpha\frac{m_0}{m}\leq E(\hat{v}(\alpha))=\alpha\frac{E(\hat{m}_0 )}{m}\leq\alpha.
nodes.statement_short: With $\hat v(\alpha)=\alpha\hat m_0/m$ and (9), $\alpha m_0/m\le E\hat v(\alpha)\le\alpha$.

nodes.name: hat v(alpha) = alpha hat m_0/m
nodes.statement: \hat{v}(\alpha)=\alpha\frac{\hat{m}_0}{m},

nodes.name: Bounds on E(hat v(alpha))
nodes.statement: \alpha\frac{m_0}{m}\leq E(\hat{v}(\alpha))=\alpha\frac{E(\hat{m}_0 )}{m}\leq\alpha.

nodes.name: Improved bound on the local-FDR estimator
nodes.statement: When using $\hat{F}(p_{(i)}) = i/m$ one gets an improved bound on the local-FDR estimator: \begin{equation} \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} m_0 \leq E \bigl(t_{(i)}\bigr) = \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} E(\hat{m}_0) \leq \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} m. \end{equation}
assumptions: When using $\hat{F}(p_{(i)}) = i/m$
conclusions: \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} m_0 \leq E \bigl(t_{(i)}\bigr) = \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} E(\hat{m}_0) \leq \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} m.
nodes.statement_short: With $\hat F(p_{(i)})=i/m$: $\frac{p_{(i)}}{i}m_0\le E\,t_{(i)}\le\frac{p_{(i)}}{i}m$.

nodes.name: Bounds on E t_(i)
nodes.statement: \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} m_0 \leq E \bigl(t_{(i)}\bigr) = \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} E(\hat{m}_0) \leq \frac{p_{(i)}}{i} m.

nodes.name: FDR control procedures with gamma_i = iq/hat m_0
nodes.statement: Procedures for FDR \textit{control}: In this approach, one wishes to control the FDR at a preset level $q$. This is achieved by defining $\gamma_i=iq/\hat{m}_0$ to be used in the same way as $\alpha_i$ and $\alpha_i^\prime$ [see equations (\ref{eq:alphadef}) and (\ref{eq:alphaprime})], leading typically to a larger number $R^\prime $ of rejected hypotheses (compared to BH95), with the $\mathit{FDR}$ still being bound by the desired value $q$.
nodes.statement_short: FDR control procedures fix level $q$ and use $\gamma_i=iq/\hat m_0$ in place of $\alpha_i$.

nodes.name: Procedures with rigorously established FDR control (BH95, BKY, STS)
nodes.statement: However, as far as we know, only for a few such procedures has control of the FDR been rigorously established: the original BH95 procedure \citet{BH95}, the two-stage and multiple-stage adaptive BH procedures \citet{BKY} (we refer to the latter as BKY), and Storey's procedure \citet{storey2002} (referred to as STS).
nodes.origin_citation: Benjamini & Hochberg 1995; Benjamini, Krieger & Yekutieli 2006; Storey 2002
conclusions: only for a few such procedures has control of the FDR been rigorously established: the original BH95 procedure \citet{BH95}, the two-stage and multiple-stage adaptive BH procedures \citet{BKY} (we refer to the latter as BKY), and Storey's procedure \citet{storey2002} (referred to as STS)
nodes.statement_short: FDR control is proven for BH95, the two-/multiple-stage adaptive BH procedures (BKY) and Storey's procedure (STS); names BKY and STS.

nodes.name: Improved BH (IBH) procedures
nodes.statement: We analyze simulated and real data, and show that for both the new procedures almost always reject more hypotheses than BH95, while maintaining control even under dependence, and we therefore refer to these procedures as ``Improved BH'' (IBH).
differentia: almost always reject more hypotheses than BH95, while maintaining control even under dependence

nodes.name: Monotonic estimator for m_0
nodes.statement: An estimator for $m_0$ is a family of functions $\hat{m}_0\equiv \hat{m}_0^{(m)}\dvtx [0,1]^m \to\mathbb{R}$, $\hat{m}_0\equiv\hat{m}_0(\vec{p})$. We usually omit the index $^{(m)}$, as it is obvious from the context. We say that $\hat{m}_0$ is a monotonic estimator if it satisfies the following: \begin{enumerate} \item$\hat{m}_0^{(m)}(p_1,\ldots,p_i,\ldots,p_m) \!\geq\! \hat{m}_0^{(m)}(p_1,\ldots,p_i',\ldots,p_m)$, $\forall p_i \geq p_i'$, $i=1,2,\ldots, m$, $ m \geq1$. \item $\hat{m}_0^{(m)}(p_1,\ldots,p_i,\ldots,p_m) \geq \hat{m}_0^{(m-1)}(p_1,\ldots,p_{i-1},p_{i+1},\ldots,p_{m})$, $ \forall i=1,2, \ldots,\break m$, $ m \geq2$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2 \texorpdfstring{Preliminaries and theorem on control.}{Preliminaries and theorem on control}
nodes.statement_short: An $m_0$-estimator is monotonic if it is nondecreasing in each p-value and does not increase when a p-value is removed.
nodes.label: def:monotonit

nodes.name: Modified step-up BH procedure with estimator hat m_0
nodes.statement: Assume w.l.o.g that we have $m$ hypotheses, the first~$m_0$ of which are null. Let $\vec{p}= (p_1,\ldots,p_m)$ be the corresponding $p$-values. The modified step-up BH procedure with estimator $\hat{m}_0$ is defined as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Compute $\hat{m}_0\equiv\hat{m}_0(\vec{p})$.\vadjust{\goodbreak} \item For each $i$ define \begin{equation} \gamma_i = \frac{i q}{\hat{m}_0} . \end{equation} \item Order the $p$-values in an increasing order: $p_{(1)} \leq\cdots \leq p_{(m)}$. \item Let $R = \max\{i\dvtx p_{(i)} \leq\gamma_i\}$, and reject the hypotheses $(1),(2),\ldots,(R)$ (if no such $R$ exists, do not reject any hypothesis). \end{enumerate} This procedure is similar to the original BH95 procedure, with the additional initial step of estimating $m_0$, and the different set of constants used to determine $R$. The modified step-down BH procedure is defined in the same way, except that in step $4$ we take $R=\min \{i\dvtx p_{(i)} >\alpha_i \} - 1$.

nodes.name: FDR bound for adaptive BH procedures with a monotonic m_0 estimator
nodes.statement: $\!\!\!$Let $\hat{m}_0\equiv\hat{m}_0(\vec{p})$ be a monotonic estimator for $m_0$. Consi\-der the modified step-up BH procedure defined above. nodes.name: The leave-one-out estimator is only auxiliary
nodes.statement: Here $p_1$ is a representative of one of the true null $p$-values. The modified estimator $\hat{m}_0^{(\not1)}$ which excludes $p_1$ cannot be implemented in practice, as the researcher does not know which of the $p$-values are null, but for any estimator $\hat{m}_0$ we can still consider this hypothetical estimator (in similar vain to the ``oracle'' procedure sometimes considered in the literature) and study its statistical properties---it only serves for a hypothetical auxiliary procedure which is used in the proof of the theorem, and the theorem applies to the practical original procedure with the estimator $\hat{m}_0$ which does use $p_1$ (as well as all other $p$-values).

nodes.name: Why small corrections to the estimators are needed
nodes.statement:
In order to show control of the FDR using Theorem ef {thm:m0_control}, we have to apply small corrections to both estimators, turning them into conservative estimators (i.e., overestimating $m_0$). This is due to two reasons: the first is that the bound on the FDR given in Theorem ef{thm:m0_control} uses $\hat{m}_0^{(
ot1)}$ (rather than $\hat{m}_0$) and, thus, we ``lose'' one of the $p$-values and need to correct for that. The second reason is that $\hat{m}_0^{(
ot1)}$ appears in the denominator, and its fluctuations have asymmetric influence on the FDR bound. This can be illustrated by using Jensen's inequality which gives $E[1/ \hat{m}_0^{(
ot1)}] \geq1 / E[\hat{m}_0^{(
ot1)}]$, thus showing that an unbiased estimator for $m_0$ will typically show a bias when its reciprocal is used. Nevertheless, we show that these two effects can be overcome by applying a small correction, which becomes negligible as the number of hypotheses goes to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: Corrections are needed because the bound uses the leave-one-out estimator and, by Jensen, the reciprocal of an unbiased estimator is biased.

nodes.statement_short: Null p-values are uniform with mean 1/2, so $E\hat m_0'\ge m_0$.

nodes.name: FDR monotonicity question
nodes.statement: Our formulation of the question in the multiple-hypothesis settings using FDR is as follows: Given two procedures, $B^{(1)}, B^{(2)}$ (possibly parameterized by $q$ or other parameters), and assuming that for any realization of the $p$-values, $B^{(2)}$ passes more hypotheses than $B^{(1)}$, is it true that $\mathit{FDR}^{(1)} \leq \mathit{FDR}^{(2)}$?
nodes.statement_short: If procedure $B^{(2)}$ always rejects at least as many hypotheses as $B^{(1)}$, is $FDR^{(1)}\le FDR^{(2)}$?

nodes.name: FDR monotonicity theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{p}= (p_{1,\ldots,m})$ be a set of independent $p$-values. Assume that $f$, the marginal probability density function of the alternatives, is monotonically nonincreasing and differentiable. Let $B^{(i)}$ be two threshold FDR procedures rejecting $R^{(i)}(\vec{p})$ hypotheses and each having $\mathit{FDR}^{(i)}$, $i=1,2$. Assume that for any $q$, $R^{(1)}(\vec{p}) \leq R^{(2)}(\vec{p}), \forall\vec{p}$. Then it also holds that $\mathit{FDR}^{(1)} \leq \mathit{FDR}^{(2)}$.

conclusions: $\mathit{FDR}^{(1)} \leq \mathit{FDR}^{(2)}$

nodes.name: Counterexample to FDR monotonicity (m=3, m_0=1)
nodes.statement:
Let $m=3$ and $m_0=1$. Let the two alternative hypotheses $p$-values be taken from a mixture distribution, $p_i \sim\varepsilon U[0,\varepsilon]+(1-\varepsilon)\delta(p_i-\varepsilon)$ for some $0 < \varepsilon< 1$. Thus, $p_2, p_3$ are ``truncated'' uniform r.v.s., having $1-\varepsilon$ of their mass concentrated at $\varepsilon$, and the rest ($\varepsilon$) uniformly distributed on $[0,\varepsilon]$; their distributions are stochastically smaller than $U[0,1]$. For simplicity of computations, we assume that $\varepsilon\ll 1$ and thus look only at the first order in $\varepsilon$, although the example's conclusion holds for any $\varepsilon> 0$. Let $P^{(1)}$ be the procedure always rejecting the lowest $p$-value and $P^{(2)}$ be the procedure rejecting the two lowest $p$-values (we assume that ties are handled in the same way by both procedures, for example, by taking $p$-values in lexicographic order---the precise tie-breaking rule does not change the example's results). We next compute the FDR for both procedures:  egin{eqnarray} \mathit{FDR}^{(1)} &=& \Pr(p_1 < p_2, p_3) = \varepsilon[ \varepsilon^2 / 3 + 2 \varepsilon(1-\varepsilon) / 2 + (1-\varepsilon)^2 ] 
onumber\[-8pt]\[-8pt] &=& \varepsilon+ O(\varepsilon^2),
onumber \ \mathit{FDR}^{(2)} &=&  igl(1 - \Pr( p_1 > p_2, p_3) igr) / 2 = [1 - (1-\varepsilon) - \varepsilon^3/3]/2 
onumber\[-8pt]\[-8pt] &=& \varepsilon/2 + O(\varepsilon^3).
onumber \end{eqnarray} Thus, for $\varepsilon$ small enough $\mathit{FDR}^{(1)} > \mathit{FDR}^{(2)}$ and the more conservative procedure leads, in fact, to a higher FDR.
nodes.statement_short: Two alternatives with mass $1-\varepsilon$ at $\varepsilon$: rejecting one p-value gives FDR $\approx\varepsilon$, rejecting two gives $\approx\varepsilon/2$.

nodes.statement: We conclude these comparisons between the different procedures by presenting, in Figure \ref{fig:comparison_EVR_and_ESm}c and d, their power, measured as the fraction of correctly rejected hypotheses, or ``True Discovery Rate.''

nodes.name: False Non-Discovery Rate
nodes.statement: This measure of power is one minus the type two error rate, known as the False Non-Discovery Rate $T/m_1$ [\citet{Genovese2002}].
nodes.section: 5.1 \texorpdfstring{Comparison of several methods under dependency.}{Comparison of several methods under dependency}

nodes.name: Power comparison (simulation)
nodes.statement: For the independent case $\rho= 0$ the power values of the ORC, BKY, STS and both IBH procedures are very close and much better than that of BH95. For $\rho= 0.8$ STS has the highest power, followed closely by the oracle, both IBH and BKY, with a large gap to BH95.
nodes.section: 5.1 \texorpdfstring{Comparison of several methods under dependency.}{Comparison of several methods under dependency}
conclusions: much better than that of BH95

nodes.name: No simple monotone relation between FDR and power (simulation)
nodes.statement: Interestingly, there is no simple monotonicity relationship between the values of the FDR, $E(V/R^+)$, and the True Discovery Rate $E(S/m_1)$.
nodes.section: 5.1 \texorpdfstring{Comparison of several methods under dependency.}{Comparison of several methods under dependency}
conclusions: there is no simple monotonicity relationship between the values of the FDR, $E(V/R^+)$, and the True Discovery Rate $E(S/m_1)$

nodes.name: Standard deviation of V/R^+ (simulation)
nodes.statement: As can be seen when the $p$-values are independent, the st.d. is very similar for all the procedures, but increases steeply as $m_0/m\rightarrow1$. In the case of dependent $p$-values, the situation becomes worse; for nearly the entire range of $m_0/m$ the coefficient of variance $\mathit{cv} = \mathit{st.d.}(V/R^+)/E(V/R^+)$ is greater than 1.
nodes.section: 5.1 \texorpdfstring{Comparison of several methods under dependency.}{Comparison of several methods under dependency}
conclusions: the st.d. is very similar for all the procedures, but increases steeply as $m_0/m\rightarrow1$

nodes.name: Summary of the simulation comparison
nodes.statement: We thus conclude that for $\rho=0$ our IBH procedures provide an expected improvement over the BH95 in terms of power and saturation of the bound and their performance is comparable to that of the other adaptive methods tested. For dependent variables STS violates the bound on $E(V/R^+)$ much more than the IBHlog and the IBHsum which violate it only slightly.
nodes.section: 5.1 \texorpdfstring{Comparison of several methods under dependency.}{Comparison of several methods under dependency}
conclusions: For dependent variables STS violates the bound on $E(V/R^+)$ much more than the IBHlog and the IBHsum which violate it only slightly

nodes.name: Probability that a single realization satisfies the level (simulation)
nodes.statement: As seen in Figure \ref{fig:m_500_q5_mu1_3p5_Pr_VR_leq_q_comparison_tex}a, the results of IBH are slightly more conservative than the oracle in the case of independence, while all improved procedures have fairly similar results. In the case of strong dependency, Figure \ref{fig:m_500_q5_mu1_3p5_Pr_VR_leq_q_comparison_tex}b, the differences between the procedures are more pronounced; the STS is the most permissive procedure.
nodes.section: 5.2 \texorpdfstring{Applicability for a particular realization.}{Applicability for a particular realization}
conclusions: the results of IBH are slightly more conservative than the oracle in the case of independence

nodes.name: Positive dependence lowers the probability of violating the bound (simulation)
nodes.statement: It is very interesting to see that in the case of positive dependent statistics the probability to violate the bound is smaller, although $E[V/R^+]$ is larger.
nodes.section: 5.2 \texorpdfstring{Applicability for a particular realization.}{Applicability for a particular realization}
assumptions: in the case of positive dependent statistics
conclusions: the probability to violate the bound is smaller, although $E[V/R^+]$ is larger

nodes.name: CDF of V/R^+ for the procedures (simulation)
nodes.statement: We would like to emphasize two points: (1) The CDFs of our improved procedures have very similar behavior to the other improved procedures. (2) While in the independent case the distribution is close to symmetric, under dependency the distribution is very nonsymmetric, and, hence, controlling the mean (of $V/R^+$) is almost irrelevant.
nodes.section: 5.2 \texorpdfstring{Applicability for a particular realization.}{Applicability for a particular realization}
conclusions: The CDFs of our improved procedures have very similar behavior to the other improved procedures

nodes.name: Leukemia data: IBHsum gives 23% more discoveries than BH95
nodes.statement: For the first data set the BH95 procedure yields at $q=0.1$ a large number of $R=0.6065 \times21\mbox{,}288 = 12\mbox{,}912$ discoveries (see Figure \ref{fig:example_pval}a). When we apply our procedure we get, at the same FDR, $R' =0.746 \cdot21\mbox{,}288 =15\mbox{,}884$ (for the \mbox{IBHsum}) discoveries, that is, 23\% more.
nodes.section: 6.1 \texorpdfstring{Detailed application of our procedures.}{Detailed application of our procedures}
conclusions: that is, 23\% more

nodes.name: Breast cancer data: IBHsum gives 24% more discoveries than BH95
nodes.statement: The BH95 procedure yields for the second data set (at $q=0.1$) $R=499$ discoveries. When we apply our procedure we get, at the same FDR, $R' = 621$ (for the IBHsum) discoveries, that is, 24\% more.
nodes.section: 6.1 \texorpdfstring{Detailed application of our procedures.}{Detailed application of our procedures}
conclusions: that is, 24\% more

nodes.name: Two-tailed data sets: STS and IBH improve more than BKY
nodes.statement: Inspection of Table \ref{table:comparison_real_data} reveals that for types (a), (b)---of two-tailed tests, irrespective of the number of discoveries and FDR level, STS and both IBH procedures give significantly higher improvement over BH95 than the BKY procedure, with STS performing slightly better than IBHlog, followed by IBHsum.
nodes.section: 6.2 \texorpdfstring{Applying our procedures to many data sets.}{Applying our procedures to many data sets}
assumptions: for types (a), (b)---of two-tailed tests
conclusions: STS and both IBH procedures give significantly higher improvement over BH95 than the BKY procedure

nodes.name: One-tailed, many discoveries: BKY best and IBHlog fails
nodes.statement: For the one-tailed test with large numbers of discoveries [type (c)] the mean improvement of BKY is the highest, while STS and IBHsum are quite similar. IBHlog fails dramatically in this case due to the abundance of $p$-values close to one, giving an over-estimation of $m_0$.
nodes.section: 6.2 \texorpdfstring{Applying our procedures to many data sets.}{Applying our procedures to many data sets}
assumptions: For the one-tailed test with large numbers of discoveries [type (c)]
conclusions: the mean improvement of BKY is the highest
IBHlog fails dramatically in this case

nodes.name: One-tailed, few discoveries: IBHsum slightly better than STS
nodes.statement: For type (d), one-tailed tests with a small number of discoveries, IBHsum is slightly better than STS and both yield a significantly higher improvement than BKY.
nodes.section: 6.2 \texorpdfstring{Applying our procedures to many data sets.}{Applying our procedures to many data sets}
assumptions: For type (d), one-tailed tests with a small number of discoveries
conclusions: IBHsum is slightly better than STS and both yield a significantly higher improvement than BKY

nodes.name: IBH improves on BH95 on all real-data comparison types
nodes.statement: In summary, our IBH procedures constitute in all cases a significant improvement over the original BH95; in all but one of the comparison types the improvement is significantly better than that of the BKY method. Comparison with STS yields mixed results, but the edge of STS over IBH in two of the four comparison types is overshadowed by the fact that STS does not provide a reliable bound for data sets with positive correlations between probe sets, while IBH remains reliable.
nodes.section: 6.2 \texorpdfstring{Applying our procedures to many data sets.}{Applying our procedures to many data sets}
conclusions: our IBH procedures constitute in all cases a significant improvement over the original BH95

nodes.name: Recommendation: IBHlog for two-tailed, IBHsum for one-tailed tests
nodes.statement: We recommend using our IBHlog procedure for two-tailed tests, and IBHsum procedure for a one-tailed test, to increase discovery power while controlling FDR levels.
